Model Monitoring with alert thresholds for training-serving skew and inference drift
A stricter safety setting, so that unusual forecasts are blocked before they ever reach planners
quiz.explain: The model is healthy but the world changed, which is drift, and Model Monitoring compares production data with a baseline and alerts when it moves past a threshold. Choice B is tempting because rolling back a version is a real lifecycle tool, but it does not tell the team that the data has changed.

days.recap: Know the six limitations: data dependency, knowledge cutoff, bias, fairness, hallucination and edge cases. Match remedies: grounding or RAG for current facts, prompt engineering first, fine-tuning for domain depth, and HITL for high-stakes output. Keep running: evaluate before upgrades, version models, track retirement dates, monitor drift and skew, watch KPIs, and use Feature Store for consistent features.

days.title: Prompt Engineering Techniques: Which Technique for Which Task

concepts.heading: What Prompt Engineering Is and Why It Matters
concepts.body: A prompt is the natural language request sent to a model. It can hold a task, instructions, background context, examples and even partial text for the model to continue. Prompt engineering is the repeated cycle of writing a prompt, checking the answer and rewriting. Its business significance is that only the input changes. The model's weights are untouched, so the technique is fast, cheap and reversible, and it needs no training data pipeline or training run. Google's prompting guide lists the parts of a strong prompt: an objective, an optional persona, instructions and constraints, tone, context, few-shot examples and an explicit output format. Clear and specific instructions come first, and missing context or a missing output format forces the model to guess. Prompt engineering improves answers but cannot guarantee that they are error free, so human review of important drafts remains good practice. A sensible order for a business is to try prompt techniques first and consider heavier customization such as fine-tuning only when prompting cannot reach the quality or consistency needed.

concepts.heading: Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Few-Shot
concepts.body: These three names count the worked examples placed inside the prompt. Zero-shot has an instruction and the input but no examples. It suits common, well-defined tasks such as summarizing a press release or translating a short notice. One-shot includes exactly one example of an input and the output you want, which is a good compromise when only one approved sample exists, for example a single release-note headline in the house style. Few-shot includes several examples, and it is mainly used to control output format, phrasing, scope and pattern. A support team that needs every email labeled with one of four fixed categories, returned in a fixed format, is a classic few-shot task, because the model understands the task but the shape of its answer varies. Start with the lightest approach that works and add examples only when the instruction cannot describe the pattern well. Always pair examples with clear instructions, and make them varied and balanced, or the model may copy unintended patterns.

concepts.heading: Role Prompting and Prompt Chaining
concepts.body: Role prompting tells the model who it is acting as, for example a patient tutor explaining mortgage terms to first-time buyers. The persona shapes vocabulary, depth, tone and point of view, while constraints state what the model must not do, such as giving personal financial advice. Instructions that should hold for the whole conversation fit best in system instructions, so users do not repeat them every turn. Prompt chaining is a different idea. It splits a complex job into a sequence of smaller prompts in which the output of one becomes the input of the next. Reading a long feedback document, extracting the main complaints, grouping them into themes and drafting an executive summary are four distinct stages, so a chain suits them. Each step has one clear goal, and you can inspect and correct output between steps. Do not confuse chaining with few-shot: chaining links separate prompts in sequence and says nothing about examples inside a prompt.

concepts.heading: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
concepts.body: Chain-of-thought prompting encourages the model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before it states a final answer. It helps on tasks where the result depends on several dependent steps, such as arithmetic with several discount rules, logic puzzles, planning or checking a long contract clause for consistency. There are two common variants. Zero-shot chain-of-thought simply adds an instruction such as think through this step by step. Few-shot chain-of-thought includes examples that show the worked reasoning followed by the answer. Order matters: the reasoning must come before the final answer, because each generated step becomes context for the next one. Examples that show the answer first and the explanation afterward teach the model to commit first and justify later, which removes the benefit. Responses get longer, so use it where accuracy matters more than brevity. Chain-of-thought reasons only with information already in the prompt and the model's training, so it cannot look anything up.

concepts.heading: ReAct and Choosing a Technique
concepts.body: ReAct, short for reason and act, has the model interleave a short line of reasoning with an action, such as calling a tool or running a search, then read the result, called an observation, and reason again. The loop repeats until it can answer. Use it when the answer depends on information or actions outside the prompt, such as live order status, inventory or today's rates, or when each step depends on the last lookup. Compare it directly with chain-of-thought: if the whole problem is in the text, reasoning is enough; if the model must look something up or act, add ReAct and give it tools. Techniques combine: a claims workflow with distinct stages of read, verify, decide and write suits a chain of prompts, and the verification stage can use ReAct to query a policy database. A quick map for the exam: common task with no special format means zero-shot; one sample means one-shot; fixed output pattern means few-shot; audience and tone means a role; stages mean chaining; multi-step logic means chain-of-thought; outside data means ReAct.

examPoints: A question that counts examples is testing zero-shot, one-shot or few-shot: none, exactly one, or several, with few-shot used mainly to control output format and pattern.

A question about breaking a job into stages whose outputs feed each other is testing prompt chaining, not few-shot; one about a wrong total on a multi-step calculation is testing chain-of-thought with reasoning before the answer.
A question where the model needs live data or must call a tool mid-task is testing ReAct, while a self-contained reasoning task over supplied text is testing chain-of-thought.

quiz.q: A support team wants every incoming email labeled as Billing, Outage, Feature Request or Account Access, returned in one fixed format. The model understands the task, but its wording varies. Which technique fits best?
choices: Prompt chaining, by sending the same email through four separate prompts in sequence
ReAct prompting, by letting the model call a ticket database before it writes each label
Zero-shot prompting, by repeating the instruction in several different styles within the prompt
Few-shot prompting, by showing several emails each followed by exactly the correct label
quiz.explain: Few-shot examples show the model the exact label vocabulary and format, which is what the task needs. Choice A is tempting because chaining also uses several prompts, but it links stages of a job and does nothing to fix the shape of one answer.

quiz.q: A claims assistant must read a claim, check each fact against a live policy database, decide whether more evidence is needed and then write a letter. Which combination of techniques fits?
choices: Prompt chaining for the distinct stages, with ReAct in the stage that must query the database
Zero-shot prompting for the whole task, with a role that tells the model it is a claims adjuster
Chain-of-thought alone, because every stage can be solved from the text of the claim
One-shot prompting with a single sample letter, because the output is a letter
quiz.explain: The job has separate stages, which suits a chain, and one stage needs outside data, which is the ReAct pattern of reason, call a tool and read the result. Choice C is tempting because the task involves reasoning, but chain-of-thought cannot fetch the policy records.

days.recap: Prompt engineering improves output by improving the input, with no change to the model. Zero-shot has no examples, one-shot has one, few-shot has several and controls format. Role prompting sets audience and tone, prompt chaining links stages, chain-of-thought puts reasoning before the answer, and ReAct adds tool use for outside data.

days.title: Grounding, RAG, and Sampling Parameters

concepts.heading: What Grounding Is
concepts.body: A foundation model answers from patterns learned in training. It has no built-in link to your documents, to today's news or to a licensed data feed, so it can produce fluent text that is wrong. Grounding connects the model's output to verifiable sources. Google's documentation lists three benefits: fewer hallucinations, answers anchored to your data sources, and auditability, because the response can point to the sources it used. A compliance team that cannot verify where a statement came from needs grounding, not a new temperature setting. Grounding does not change the model's weights, does not limit the model to canned text and is not a network or hosting setting. It supplies trustworthy material at the time of the request. Grounded answers also inherit the quality of the sources. If an obsolete policy stays in the index, the model can quote it, and the fix is to retire or update the source documents and give owners a process for keeping them current, not to change generation settings.

concepts.heading: Enterprise, Third-Party, and World Data
concepts.body: The guide asks you to tell three kinds of grounding data apart. Enterprise data, also called first-party data, is content your organization owns, such as policies, manuals, contracts, product catalogs and records in your databases and document stores. Third-party data comes from outside providers that you license or connect to, such as a market-data feed, a partner catalog or an external search service that already runs over licensed content. World data is broad public knowledge, such as what a search engine returns for current events and general topics. Ask who owns the facts and how often they change. Internal lending rules are yours. A paid research feed belongs to a provider and may be best used through the provider's own search service at request time instead of being copied. This week's flight disruptions are public and change daily, so a snapshot of company files would be stale. The right source follows where the facts live, and one assistant can use more than one source.

concepts.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Its Effect on Output
concepts.body: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, adds a lookup step before the model writes. The user asks a question, a retrieval step searches a knowledge source, often a search index or a vector store of document chunks, and returns the most relevant passages. Those passages are added to the prompt as context, and the model generates an answer that uses the supplied material. The system can also show which sources were used. The effect on output is that the model works from current, specific text instead of training memory alone, so answers are more accurate for your data, less likely to be invented and easier to check. The weights never change, so new documents become usable as soon as they are indexed, and updating knowledge means refreshing the index rather than retraining. RAG does not remove the need for good sources or human review of high-stakes content. It is also the better fit than fine-tuning when documents change often and answers must cite them.

concepts.heading: Google Cloud Grounding Offerings
concepts.body: Google Cloud gives several routes. Pre-built RAG with Agent Search is a managed search-and-answer experience: you point it at websites or documents and it handles ingestion, indexing, retrieval and answer generation, so it is the quicker, low-effort route. The RAG APIs, with RAG Engine, are a configurable managed service for developers who want to shape the pipeline, such as how data is parsed and retrieved, and combine it with their own application logic. Grounding with Google Search connects the model to world knowledge using results from Google's search engine, which suits public, fast-changing information the company does not own. Other options connect Gemini to an existing external index, such as Elasticsearch, or to any search API, which suits third-party data that should stay where its owner keeps it. The decision trade is speed and low effort versus control: quick managed answers over content point to pre-built RAG, custom pipeline control points to the RAG APIs, and public current facts point to Google Search.

concepts.heading: Sampling Parameters and Settings
concepts.body: Sampling settings control how a model writes, not which facts it has. When a model writes it picks each next token from a probability distribution. Temperature controls how random that pick is: lower values choose the most probable tokens more often, giving focused, predictable output suited to fee explanations or dosing documents, while higher values give more diverse, creative output suited to slogans and brainstorming. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, narrows the candidate tokens to the most probable ones whose probabilities add up to the top-p value, and temperature then applies to those that remain; a lower top-p is less random and a higher one more random. Maximum output tokens, the output length setting, caps how many tokens a response may contain, so an answer that stops mid-sentence usually hit that cap. A token is a small piece of text, roughly a few characters. Token counts also affect cost and speed. Safety settings choose how aggressively harmful categories are blocked, though some protections are always on. For accuracy tasks combine grounding with low randomness; length caps and safety filters do neither job.

examPoints: A question about answers that cannot be traced to a source is testing grounding or RAG, which adds citations and auditability, not temperature, length or safety settings.

A question that lists internal documents, a licensed provider's search service and current public news is testing enterprise, third-party and world data, with Agent Search or RAG Engine, an external search connection, and Grounding with Google Search as the matching offerings.
A question about repeatable factual wording versus varied creative ideas is testing temperature and top-p, while a response cut off mid-sentence is testing maximum output tokens.

quiz.q: A government agency wants an intranet question-answering assistant live quickly, with Google handling indexing, retrieval and answer generation over its websites. Which offering fits?
choices: RAG APIs, so developers can tune how documents are parsed and retrieved
Grounding with Google Search, so answers come from the public web
Pre-built RAG with Agent Search, which manages ingestion and answers
A higher temperature setting, so the model produces a wider range of answers
quiz.explain: Pre-built RAG with Agent Search is the managed, low-effort route that handles ingestion, indexing, retrieval and answer generation. Choice A is tempting because RAG APIs are also managed RAG, but they suit teams that want control over the pipeline and are willing to build more.

quiz.q: A bank's assistant explains fee schedules, and every answer must stay consistent and close to the supplied policy text. Pilot answers vary in wording from run to run. Which adjustment helps most?
choices: Raise the temperature so the model can explore more varied phrasings of each rule
Lower the temperature and keep the answers grounded in the policy text
Reduce maximum output tokens so that each explanation becomes much shorter
Loosen the safety settings so the model can quote the policy more directly
quiz.explain: Lower temperature makes the most probable tokens more likely, giving focused and more repeatable wording, and grounding keeps the facts tied to the policy. Choice C is tempting because shorter answers vary less, but a length cap only truncates output and can drop important qualifiers.

days.recap: Grounding ties output to verifiable sources, cutting hallucination and adding traceability; it depends on good source data. Know enterprise, third-party and world data. RAG retrieves passages and adds them to the prompt. Offerings: pre-built RAG with Agent Search, RAG APIs, and Grounding with Google Search. Low temperature or top-p is focused, high is creative; output tokens cap length; safety settings block harm.

days.title: Implementing a Gen AI Solution and Securing AI

concepts.heading: Types of Solutions and Business versus Technical Factors
concepts.body: Ready-made applications, such as Gemini for Google Workspace or Gemini Enterprise, are assistants that employees use directly with little or no engineering. Configured or low-code solutions point pre-built products such as search or conversational agents at your own data or processes. Custom solutions are applications and agents built on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, where the team chooses models, grounding and evaluation. Model-level work such as fine-tuning needs the most data, skills and time. Content types (text, image, code, personalized experiences) each point to a model suited to that output. Two lists drive any decision. Business requirements say what outcome is wanted and how success is judged, such as faster resolution, a launch date or a budget. Technical constraints are the conditions to live within: data state and format, response speed, systems to integrate with, and security or residency rules. Requirements decide what is worth building; constraints decide what is feasible.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Solution
concepts.body: Start with the problem, not the technology. Google Cloud's guidance says to understand the business problem and required outcomes first, then break the objectives into measurable KPIs. Then match the need to a pattern. Questions over the company's own documents, with citations, point to grounding or RAG, for example Agent Search or a custom RAG application. Content creation points to a generative model. Large numbers of customer conversations point to conversational agents. Common tasks such as meeting summaries and routine emails point to a ready-made assistant, especially with no data science team and a need for quick results. Google's cost guidance recommends an incremental approach: begin with managed services and pre-trained models, look in Model Garden for models that already do the job, test with prompting, and add grounding or tuning only when evaluation shows a gap. Building from scratch is reserved for needs nothing pre-built can meet. Scattered or duplicated files may need processing first.

concepts.heading: Integrating Gen AI into the Organization and Measuring Impact
concepts.body: A common order: identify the problem, define KPIs and the current baseline, check data and technical fit, choose a solution, pilot with a limited lower-risk group, integrate, then expand what works. Good pilots have measurable outcomes, governed data and contained users. A successful rollout combines people, governance, process and measurement: training and champions, data-use policies developed with security, legal and IT teams, workflow changes, and the pilot's KPIs. Google Cloud describes three families of measures: model quality (how good the output is), system quality (latency, errors, uptime) and business operational measures (effect on work, such as containment rate, handle time, satisfaction and cost per task). Good scores with little use mean little impact, so add adoption and feedback; KPIs can pull against each other, so judge them together.

concepts.heading: Security Across the ML Lifecycle and SAIF
concepts.body: Secure AI means protecting AI systems from attacks and misuse. Google Cloud asks for a holistic approach that starts at the initial concept and runs through development, deployment and operations, because adding controls early is easier than adding them later. At the plan stage, define security goals and consider risks such as data poisoning, model inversion and adversarial attacks. At the data stage, protect training data and de-identify sensitive values. At build time, secure pipelines and use least-privilege identities. At run time, screen prompts and responses, monitor, audit and be ready to respond. Google's Secure AI Framework, SAIF, is a conceptual framework for securing AI systems; its resources include an introduction, a risk self-assessment that shows which AI-specific risks may affect you, and guidance on applying it across the AI development lifecycle. For the exam, SAIF is guidance, not a product: learn which risks apply, then pick the tools that carry out the controls.

concepts.heading: Google Cloud Security Tools for AI
concepts.body: Match each tool to its purpose. IAM controls who can do what on which resource: use narrow predefined roles at the smallest scope, not broad basic roles in production. Security Command Center is Google Cloud's risk management solution, and its AI Protection capability manages the security posture of AI workloads: an AI asset inventory (including shadow AI), risks, over-privileged agents, compliance and threat detection, which suits an enterprise-wide view. Model Armor screens individual prompts and responses at run time for prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage and harmful content. Sensitive Data Protection discovers and de-identifies sensitive data before it reaches training, tuning or prompts. Customer-managed encryption keys in Cloud KMS and perimeters such as VPC Service Controls protect data and model files from theft. Secure by design means building controls in across the lifecycle, secure by default means settings start protected, and defense in depth means no single control is enough.

examPoints: A question about a company with no data science team that wants fewer hours writing summaries and emails is testing the lightest solution type, a ready-made assistant, before any custom build.

A question that asks for a measure of business impact is testing operational KPIs measured against a baseline, not model quality scores or system latency alone; good test scores with low usage point to adoption and feedback.

A question that names a risk is testing the matching tool: an organization-wide view of AI assets and threats is Security Command Center AI Protection, screening prompts and responses is Model Armor, who may call a service is IAM, and sensitive values in training data is Sensitive Data Protection.

quiz.q: A bank's security team suspects that business units have deployed AI models and agents on Google Cloud without telling anyone. It wants one view of AI assets, risks and threats across the organization. Which tool fits?
choices: Model Armor, which screens each prompt and response for injection as they happen
Sensitive Data Protection, which finds and de-identifies personal data in the files used for tuning
Cloud KMS keys, which give the bank control over how its stored model files are encrypted
Security Command Center AI Protection, which covers AI assets, risks and threats
quiz.explain: AI Protection in Security Command Center manages the security posture of AI workloads, including an inventory of AI assets and detection of risks and threats. Choice A is tempting because it is also an AI security service, but Model Armor inspects conversations at run time rather than inventorying deployments.

quiz.q: After a successful pilot, a company plans wider use of a gen AI writing assistant. Leaders ask what most helps the tool fit the organization. Which approach fits?
choices: Train users, gather feedback, involve security, legal and IT, and keep measuring KPIs
Switch off the pilot KPIs now that the tool works, so teams stop writing reports
Roll out immediately to every team and let staff work out how it fits their tasks
Rely on the high pilot quality scores as proof that wide adoption will succeed
quiz.explain: Integration combines people, governance, process and continued measurement against the baseline. Choice D is tempting because strong quality scores are a good sign, but model quality alone does not show adoption or business impact.

days.recap: Choose the lightest solution that meets the business requirements within the technical constraints: ready-made, configured, custom, then model-level. Start with the problem and KPIs, pilot, integrate with training and governance, and measure business impact against a baseline. Secure AI across the lifecycle with SAIF as guidance, IAM, Security Command Center AI Protection, Model Armor and Sensitive Data Protection.

days.title: Responsible AI: Transparency, Privacy, Fairness, and Accountability

concepts.heading: Why Responsible AI Is a Business Topic
concepts.body: Responsible AI means designing, building and operating AI so that it is safe, fair, private, transparent and accountable. Google Cloud presents it as values-based AI that is good for business, not only compliance. Stated benefits are safer, more accountable products, customer trust and a culture of responsible innovation. Lack of trust is a growing barrier to enterprise AI adoption, and organizations increasingly choose products by a provider's AI commitments. Google applies its AI Principles through review bodies that assess risks and opportunities, and a customer can borrow the idea by reviewing before launch instead of after an incident. When a board asks why to spend time on reviews, documentation and testing while competitors ship quickly, the strong answer is that these steps protect customers and the brand, build trust and reduce costly failures; they are part of delivering a reliable product, not a brake on it.

concepts.heading: Transparency
concepts.body: Transparency means being open about what an AI system is for, how it was built and tested, and where it can go wrong. Google Cloud points to resources that give model transparency in a structured, accessible way. Model Cards are short documents describing intended use, performance and limitations. Explainable AI (documented as Vertex Explainable AI) gives insight into why a model produced a result. Transparency does not mean exposing raw training data, which may contain private information; it means honest documentation about purpose, evaluation and limits. A health insurer's gen AI claims assistant should tell members and auditors what it is meant to do, how it was evaluated and what it cannot do; marketing that omits limits misleads. Telling users they are talking to AI, and how to reach a person, is part of the same principle.

concepts.heading: Privacy: Anonymization versus Pseudonymization
concepts.body: Prompts, retrieved documents and training data can contain personally identifiable information. Privacy risks include sending personal data to a provider without a clear basis, reuse for purposes the person never agreed to, sensitive details in outputs shown to the wrong people, and tuning on personal data that the model may reproduce. Expect a clear policy on what may be entered into which tool, data minimization, de-identification before use, access controls and agreements on how the provider handles your data. Sensitive Data Protection can discover and de-identify sensitive elements. Two ideas are often confused. Anonymization removes or transforms identifying information so individuals cannot reasonably be identified again; it is meant to be irreversible, and removing names alone is not enough. Pseudonymization replaces identifying values with tokens; the same input gives the same token, which keeps joins across tables working. Two-way tokens can be reversed with a key, so the data often stays personal data. Choose anonymization when nobody needs to re-identify, and pseudonymization when your own team needs a controlled way back.

concepts.heading: Data Quality, Bias, and Fairness
concepts.body: A model learns patterns from its data. If some groups are under-represented or historical decisions were skewed, the model can give those groups worse outcomes, so representativeness is a data quality dimension with direct fairness consequences. Bias is a systematic skew in data, model or process that favors or disadvantages certain people, from samples, labels, problem framing or output use. Fairness is the goal of avoiding unjust impact on people, especially across sensitive characteristics such as race, gender, age or disability. Google's AI Principles call for avoiding unfair bias. Good practice is to evaluate by subgroup, because an overall metric can hide poor results for a minority group, improve or rebalance the data, review labels for historical bias, and keep humans involved in high-impact decisions such as lending or hiring. Deleting a group from the data does not create fairness; it worsens representation. Fairness must be measured and monitored for the actual use.

concepts.heading: Accountability and Explainability
concepts.body: Accountability means that people and organizations, not models, answer for what an AI system does. In practice that means named owners, governance such as review boards or approval before launch, documentation and logging so decisions can be audited, human oversight for decisions that affect people, and a way for users to appeal or report problems. Responsibility is shared: a provider answers for its platform and models, but the company deploying an application decides the use case, prompts, data and guardrails, so it stays answerable for the application. Explainability is the ability to describe why a model produced a particular output in terms people can understand. Explainable AI offers feature-based explanations, which show how much each input contributed to a prediction, and example-based explanations, which return similar training examples. A bank asked which factors drove a credit decision needs feature attributions. With gen AI, a rationale written by a language model may not reflect the real cause of an output, so it is not an audit trail.

examPoints: A question about a model that treats rural applicants worse because they are rare in historical data is testing data quality and fairness: improve representation, evaluate by subgroup and keep humans involved, not delete the group or trust the overall metric.

A question about replacing customer IDs with tokens that can be reversed with a key is testing pseudonymization, while a question about releasing data where nobody must ever be re-identified is testing anonymization.

A question asking which factors drove an individual decision is testing explainability and Explainable AI feature attributions, whereas a question asking who answers for the outcome is testing accountability, which belongs to named people and governance.

quiz.q: A lender wants its analysts to join loan records across several tables using customer tokens, and its fraud team must be able to reverse a token when needed, using a protected key. Which approach fits?
choices: Anonymization that irreversibly removes identifiers, so that nobody can ever link the records back
Pseudonymization with reversible tokens, which keeps the same token for the same customer
Dropping all customer columns, so that the analysts have only totals and no row-level data
Publishing the loan records openly, because customer IDs alone are not personal information
quiz.explain: Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with consistent tokens, which preserves joins, and two-way tokens can be reversed with a key. Choice A is tempting because anonymization is the stronger privacy step, but it is meant to be irreversible, so the fraud team could never go back.

quiz.q: A bank must tell regulators and customers which factors, such as income and payment history, drove each credit-limit decision from its machine learning model. Which capability fits?
choices: Model Cards, which describe the model's intended use and limits in a single short document
Safety settings, which block the harmful categories of content that a model could produce
Feature-based explanations from Explainable AI, which show how much each input contributed
A higher temperature, which makes the model show a wider range of possible decisions
quiz.explain: Feature attributions show how much each input contributed to a prediction, which answers which factors drove a decision. Choice A is tempting because Model Cards support transparency, but they describe the model in general and do not explain an individual result.

days.recap: Responsible AI is good for business: safer products, customer trust and responsible innovation. Transparency means honest documentation such as Model Cards. Anonymization is irreversible while pseudonymization uses tokens that may be reversed with a key. Data quality shapes bias and fairness, so evaluate by subgroup. People are accountable for AI outcomes, and Explainable AI shows why a model produced a result.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, Commonly Confused Pairs, and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: The Generative AI Leader exam gives you 90 minutes for 50 to 60 multiple choice questions. Google does not publish a pass mark, and the result is simply pass or fail. The credential is valid for 3 years. The exam is business level: it tests whether you can choose the right product, approach or practice for a business need, and it does not ask for code, commands or console steps. The four sections are Fundamentals of gen AI at about 30 percent, Google Cloud's gen AI offerings at about 35 percent, Techniques to improve gen AI model output at about 20 percent, and Business strategies for a successful gen AI solution at about 15 percent. The offerings section is the largest, so know the products and what each is for. The exam page notes that the exam was recently updated for branding changes, so use current product names such as Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Search and Cloud Run functions.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Fundamentals and Offerings
concepts.body: Look-alike pairs cause many mistakes in the two largest sections. Supervised learning uses labeled data, unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Structured data fits rows and columns, while unstructured data such as text, images and video has no fixed schema. Prompt engineering changes only the input, while fine-tuning changes how the model behaves through additional training. Gemini is Google's multimodal model family, Gemma is an open model family, Imagen generates and edits images and Veo generates video. Gemini for Google Workspace is an assistant built into Workspace apps for end users, while Gemini Enterprise is an agent and search experience for employees across company data. Model Garden is a catalog for discovering models, while Agent Platform AutoML trains predictive models on your labeled data. Agent Search is a managed search-and-answer product, while Conversational Agents builds chat and voice agents. In the Customer Engagement Suite, Agent Assist helps a live human representative and Conversational Insights analyzes finished conversations. Google AI Studio is for quick prototyping, while Agent Studio is for governed enterprise agents.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Techniques and Business Strategy
concepts.body: Section three and four pairs are about the problem versus the fix. Knowledge cutoff means stale facts and is fixed by grounding, while hallucination means invented content and is reduced by grounding, prompts and review. Drift means the real-world data changed over time, while training-serving skew means production data differs from the training data. Zero-shot has no examples, one-shot has one and few-shot has several. Prompt chaining links separate prompts in stages, chain-of-thought puts reasoning before the answer, and ReAct adds tools to reasoning. Enterprise data is yours, third-party data is licensed and world data is public. Pre-built RAG with Agent Search is quick and managed, while the RAG APIs offer control. Temperature and top-p control randomness, maximum output tokens controls length, and safety settings block harmful content. Business requirements state the outcome and technical constraints state the limits. Model quality, system quality and business operational KPIs answer different questions. SAIF is guidance, Security Command Center AI Protection gives an organization-wide view of AI assets, Model Armor screens prompts and responses, IAM controls access and Sensitive Data Protection de-identifies data. Anonymization is irreversible, pseudonymization is reversible with a key.

concepts.heading: Use an Error Log
concepts.body: For every practice question you miss or guess, write down the pair of ideas you confused, such as Agent Assist versus Conversational Insights, drift versus skew, or Model Armor versus Security Command Center, and the clue in the stem that should have decided it. Reviewing pairs is faster than rereading every day because confusions repeat. Spend the most time on Google Cloud's offerings and fundamentals, which together are about two thirds of the exam, unless your log shows a clear weak spot elsewhere. Read each scenario for its deciding phrase before looking at the choices, such as no data science team, answers must cite sources, must be reversible, or organization-wide view. Then eliminate choices that solve a different problem. Watch for retired or outdated options in distractors: Cloud Functions is now Cloud Run functions, Vertex AI is now part of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and the Video Intelligence API is deprecated in favor of multimodal Gemini models.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan and Retake Policy
concepts.body: Check your room, webcam and system, or arrive early, well before the start time. Read the exam instructions carefully, because they explain how questions work and whether you can return to them later. Answer what you know first and mark uncertain questions for review where allowed. With 90 minutes and up to 60 questions, check the timer now and then rather than spending long on one item. Because the pass mark is not published, aim to answer every question rather than to hit a particular count, and make sure no question is left blank before you finish. If you do not pass, check Google's certification retake policy before booking another attempt, because waiting periods and rules can change.

examPoints: A question that lists look-alike Google Cloud products is testing the purpose of each, such as Gemini Enterprise for employees versus Agent Search for managed retrieval, or Google AI Studio for prototyping versus Agent Studio for governed agents.

A question that describes a symptom is testing the limitation or monitoring term behind it: stale answers are the knowledge cutoff, invented citations are hallucination, and accuracy that fades while the service is healthy is drift.

A question that names a risk or privacy need is testing the matching security or responsible AI idea: Model Armor for prompts and responses, Security Command Center AI Protection for AI posture, anonymization for irreversible removal and pseudonymization for reversible tokens.

quiz.q: A learner mixes up two security tools. Which statement correctly separates Model Armor from Security Command Center AI Protection?
choices: Model Armor screens prompts and responses at run time; AI Protection covers AI posture across the organization
Model Armor inventories AI assets across all projects; AI Protection screens each prompt and response for injection
Model Armor and AI Protection both control who can call a model, but only AI Protection can edit prompts
Model Armor encrypts model files with customer-managed keys; AI Protection filters harmful output text
quiz.explain: Model Armor inspects the content of individual conversations as they happen, while AI Protection in Security Command Center looks at the security posture of AI workloads across the organization. Choice B is tempting because it names both real behaviors, but it swaps them between the two tools.

quiz.q: A company's assistant is accurate in testing, but months after launch its answers about new products are wrong, although the service responds quickly. The knowledge it relies on changes weekly. What is the best fix?
choices: Raise the temperature so the model produces more varied answers about the new products
Fine-tune the model once on a snapshot of the catalog, so that it remembers every product
Ground the assistant in the current catalog with RAG, and keep that source updated
Reduce the maximum output tokens, so that each answer contains fewer claims to check
quiz.explain: Facts that change often belong in a live source that the model retrieves at request time, and grounding or RAG does this without retraining. Choice B is tempting because fine-tuning can add knowledge, but a snapshot is stale again within weeks.

days.recap: The exam is 90 minutes with 50 to 60 multiple choice questions, no published pass mark and 3 years of validity. Drill the confused pairs across all four sections, keep an error log of the clues you missed, answer every question, and check Google's certification retake policy before booking another attempt.
